teaser: Seven men lean over a corpse, and almost none of them is looking at it.
review_notes:
One public dissection per year permitted to the Amsterdam surgeons' guild.
Corpse: Adriaen Adriaensz, known as Aris Kindt, hanged in January 1632 for robbery (sources differ on the day of the dissection: 16 or 31 January).
Sheet held by the man behind Tulp originally showed an anatomical drawing; list of names added later.
Tulp born Claes Pietersz; name taken from the tulip sign on his house; later burgomaster of Amsterdam.
Purchase by King William I in 1828 after the guild's widows' fund planned to sell it.
2006 reconstruction of the dissection by Dutch researchers, which found small discrepancies in the forearm anatomy.
Size 169.5 x 216.5 cm. Rembrandt aged 25 (born July 1606).
Gaze directions in the tour are my reading of the image.

lesson.text: One. That is how many public dissections the surgeons of Amsterdam were allowed each year. It had to be winter, so the cold would slow the smell. The body had to be that of an executed criminal. And the event was a show: people bought tickets to watch.

In January 1632 the body belonged to Adriaen Adriaensz, known as Aris Kindt, hanged for robbery. The lecturer was Dr. Nicolaes Tulp, the city's official anatomist. And the painter hired to record the occasion was a newcomer from Leiden, 25 years old, who had never painted a group portrait.

The surgeons' guild, their professional association, already owned several anatomy portraits. In the older ones the members sit in tidy rows and stare out, with a body laid in front like a prop. Each man paid for his place and wanted his face shown clearly.
Rembrandt gave them their faces. But he also gave them something to do. Before you read on, try to work out what each man is paying attention to.

lesson.title: Who looks where
lesson.text: Seven men, one corpse. Check their eyes one by one.

spots.title: The two leaners
spots.text: These two crane forward so far their collars nearly touch. Their eyes aim past the body, toward Tulp's hands and the corner beyond. They are trying not to miss a word.

spots.title: The man at the top
spots.text: He looks straight out at you, the way sitters did in the old row-of-heads portraits. He seems to be posing rather than listening.

spots.title: The left edge
spots.text: Two men in profile, pressed against the frame. They face the lesson but have the worst seats, far from the action.

spots.title: Dr. Tulp
spots.text: The only man with a hat, a sign of his rank. He looks at none of them. His eyes go over their heads, to an audience we cannot see.

lesson.text: That is what was new. The men are held together by an event. Each one reacts to it in his own way, and a row of likenesses turns into a scene with a before and an after. No Dutch group portrait had been built like this.

Nicolaes Tulp was born Claes Pietersz. He took his new surname from the tulip on the sign of his house, “tulp” in Dutch, at the time when the flower was becoming an obsession in Holland. He later served as burgomaster, or mayor, of Amsterdam.
Now the lesson itself. Tulp is explaining how the hand works. With his right hand he holds an instrument. With his left he does something a teacher still does today when words are not enough.
Tulp is lifting the muscles of the forearm with a pair of forceps. Find the steel tips.

spots.title: The forceps
spots.text: He pinches the muscles and tendons that bend the fingers. Above them, his own left hand curls its fingers in the same movement. The dead arm shows the parts and the living hand shows what they do.

lesson.text: Here Rembrandt bent the truth. A real dissection began with the belly, because the organs rot first. This belly is untouched and only the arm is open. A slit abdomen would have made an ugly picture. A hand suited a guild of surgeons, and it suited a painter too, since both professions depend on it.

In 2006, Dutch researchers repeated the dissection on a male body to test the painting. Most of the forearm matched, with a few differences. Rembrandt may have painted that arm from a separate preparation or from an anatomy book, not from Kindt's body on the day.
The rest of the picture is built around that pale body. It is far brighter than anything else in the room, and the dark suits press in around it.
Three shapes hold the scene together.

lines.label: A pyramid of heads
lines.text: The seven surgeons are stacked into a triangle on the left, with the man who looks at you at its tip. The whole group pushes toward Tulp.

lines.label: The body
lines.text: The corpse lies on a slant, feet toward you. This shortening of a form seen end-on is called foreshortening, and it pulls you into the room.

lines.label: Arm to book
lines.text: Continue the line of the opened arm and you land on the big book propped in the corner, most likely an anatomy textbook. What the knife shows, the book confirms.

lesson.text: Did you notice the face of the dead man while the lines were drawing? Half of it lies under a soft shadow, cast by the surgeons bending over him. It is the gentlest passage in the painting, given to a man the city had just hanged.
Rembrandt's idea was to paint what a group was doing, a shared moment of attention. Every later group portrait that tells a story owes something to this room.

There is one more piece of bookkeeping in the picture. The surgeons paid by the head, and they wanted to be identified. Roam around the canvas and you will find how that was solved, along with the painter's own name.

spots.title: The list
spots.text: The man behind Tulp holds a sheet of paper. It first showed an anatomical drawing. Later the names of the sitters were written over it, and it became a roll call.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: On the wall: “Rembrandt f. 1632.” He was among the first Dutch painters to sign with his first name alone, as Raphael and Titian had done in Italy.

spots.title: The shadowed face
spots.text: Mouth slightly open, eyes in shade. Kindt was a real person with a name and a record, which is rare for a body in an anatomy picture.

spots.title: The teaching hand
spots.text: Tulp's left hand, thumb and fingers curled. He is demonstrating with living fingers the motion that the exposed tendons produce.

spots.title: The opened forearm
spots.text: Red muscle and pale tendons fan out toward the fingers. It is the only strong color in a painting of blacks, whites and grays.

spots.title: The big book
spots.text: Propped open at the feet of the corpse. It stands for the written knowledge of anatomy, which Tulp is checking against the body itself.

spots.title: The feet
spots.text: Soles toward you, sharply foreshortened. They look almost too large because they are the part of him nearest to you.

lesson.text: The painting hung in the surgeons' guild rooms for nearly two centuries. In 1828 the guild's widows' fund wanted to sell it at auction. King William I stepped in and bought it for his museum in The Hague, the Mauritshuis, where it still is.

The commission launched Rembrandt in Amsterdam, and within a few years he was the most sought-after portrait painter in the city. The canvas is about 1.7 by 2.2 meters (roughly 5 ft 7 in by 7 ft 1 in). He had fitted eight portraits into it, one dead man, and a lesson you can still follow.

quiz.question: How many public dissections could the Amsterdam surgeons hold each year?
quiz.explanation: One a year, in winter, on the body of an executed criminal.

quiz.question: What is Tulp demonstrating?
options: How muscles and tendons move the fingers
How to set a broken leg
quiz.explanation: He lifts the forearm muscles with forceps and copies the motion with his own hand.

quiz.question: In what way does the scene differ from a real dissection?
options: A real one started with the belly
A real one was done outdoors
A real one used a living patient
quiz.explanation: Organs rot first, so real dissections began with the abdomen.

quiz.question: What does the sheet of paper held behind Tulp show today?
quiz.explanation: The names were written over an earlier anatomical drawing.

quiz.question: Where did Nicolaes Tulp get his surname?
options: From a tulip on his house sign
quiz.explanation: Born Claes Pietersz, he took the name from the tulip on his house.

quiz.question: Who is the only man wearing a hat?
options: The man on the far left
quiz.explanation: The hat marks Tulp's rank as the lecturer.

facts.text: Rembrandt was about 25 and had never painted a group portrait before this one.
facts.explanation: It was his first, painted shortly after he arrived from Leiden.

facts.text: The corpse in the painting is an invented figure with no known identity.
facts.explanation: He was Adriaen Adriaensz, called Aris Kindt, hanged for robbery.

facts.text: The painting has always belonged to the Mauritshuis.
facts.explanation: It hung in the surgeons' guild until King William I bought it in 1828.
